xu2002.cite: X. Xu, Phase explosion and its time lag in nanosecond laser ablation, Appl. Surf. Sci. 197-198 (2002) 61-66, doi 10.1016/S0169-4332(02)00304-5 (PII S0169-4332(02)00304-5)
xu2002.copy: /home/treefor/projects/.workspace/outputs/ss304-phase-thermal-owner-v1.2-20261031/source-cache/purdue2002/paper.pdf (sha256 cfb42eb47e13fa94ce403be6b27aeb2183036ff7895b2eeddfc5e36e24419323; author's copy from the Purdue repository); text extract paper.txt (sha256 635d0120d99b0de19bb2c083b31cb8896eb75447a054ba2d505c0559d4667a54)
xu2002.statement: Section 2, after the Doring-Volmer homogeneous nucleation rate (Eq. 2, Skripov 1974): 'During pulsed laser heating, the amount of nuclei generated by spontaneous nucleation is negligible at temperatures lower than 0.9Tc. At a temperature of about 0.9Tc, a significant number of nuclei can be formed. Hence, explosive phase change occurs'. Section 3.1: 'the surface temperature during phase explosion is about 0.9Tc' (constant measured surface temperature above about 5 J/cm2 on nickel).
xu2002.use: primary source of the 0.9 T_c phase-explosion convention (v1.1 O6 closed); the onset is exponential in temperature through the nucleation rate, so the fraction is a threshold convention of the order of a few per cent, not a sharp material constant; Xu also reports a nucleation time lag of about 5 ns that the owner does not model (a cell reaching 0.9 T_c is refused at once)

cezairliyan1980.cite: A. Cezairliyan, A. P. Miiller, Thermophysical measurements on low carbon 304 stainless steel above 1400 K by a transient (subsecond) technique, Int. J. Thermophys. 1 (1980) 83-95, doi 10.1007/BF00506274
cezairliyan1980.value: hemispherical total emittance 0.37 (5 %); melting point 1707 K; normal spectral emittance 0.385 at 653 nm at melting
cezairliyan1980.range_check_v1_2: two indexed copies of the abstract give the 0.37 value for 1700-1900 K, with the heat capacity and resistivity measured over 1400-1700 K; one index summary attributed the emittance to the 1400-1700 K measurement range; full text not accessed. Stated range used here: 1700-1900 K (solid near melting and the start of the liquid).
cezairliyan1980.use: emissivity 0.37 for solid and liquid at all temperatures; outside 1700-1900 K it is extrapolated (model_derived); Roger, Yen & Ramanathan 1979 (cited in DATA-SOURCES-v1.1.json) measured the temperature variation for solid 304 and were not read for values

critical_points.cite: Sjostrom 2023 (304L EOS, 9500 K); Mattsson & Desjarlais 2004 (steel QMD, 10000 K at 2 g/cc, about 2000 K above SESAME 4272)
critical_points.use: unchanged default T_c = 8000 K (the SESAME 4272 value as stated by Mattsson & Desjarlais 2004, the lowest estimate cited): explosion temperature 0.9 T_c = 7200 K, above the 6000 K law domain; nothing better was found in this round

stoker1957.cite: J. J. Stoker, Water Waves, Interscience, New York (1957) (dam break on a wet bed: rarefaction, constant middle state, bore satisfying the jump conditions)
stoker1957.use: analytic reference of the dam-break benchmark (method reference)

audusse2004.cite: E. Audusse, F. Bouchut, M.-O. Bristeau, R. Klein, B. Perthame, A fast and stable well-balanced scheme with hydrostatic reconstruction for shallow water flows, SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 25 (2004) 2050-2065, doi 10.1137/S1064827503431090
